newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lawmaker presses for Friday vote to oust Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Lawmaker presses for Friday vote to oust Yeltsin.

text.p: Russia's communists stepped up efforts to oust ailing President Boris Yeltsin on Wednesday and a leading parliamentarian said he would press for a vote to force the president from office on grounds of ill health.

Viktor Ilyukhin launched his initiative as the legal department of the lower house, the State Duma, issued a statement saying that such a vote would not have legal force. But it added that parliament should pass a law setting down a proceedure for removing the head of state on health grounds.
Ilyukhin led the proposal through the Security Committee which he chairs and he told reporters he would press the Duma to vote on the measure on Friday.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said the party would decide on Thursday whether to support the proposal, but he appeared to give it his backing.
"I consider the initiative well-founded and completely understandable," Zyuganov, whose party is the largest in the Duma, told a news conference.
The Russian constitution is vague on removing an ailing head of state, saying only that the president "ceases his functions" if his health is too weak to remain in office.
It does not specify who determines whether the president is too ill or who makes the final decision that he must step down.
Yeltsin, 65, must spend the rest of the week in hospital with pneumonia in both lungs, the Kremlin's chief doctor said on Wednesday, adding that his condition had "stabilised" in recent days.
Since being re-elected last July, heart trouble and a coronary bypass operation in November have kept Yeltsin out of the Kremlin for all but a few days.

"The president last year worked four months -- only during the election campaign -- and on the whole he didn't focus on government affairs but on promises," said Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in last July's presidential contest.
"For any citizen of the country it raises the question: 'Why isn't there any leadership in the country?'" he said.
The Duma's communist chairman said Yeltsin's poor health had caused a profound social crisis.
"We are seeing a systemic crisis in the state, which is manifested in a crisis of authority," Gennady Seleznyov told the Duma at its first session following the New Year recess.
"It is mainly because the functioning of the institution of the presidency has got out of line," he said.
Seleznyov's speech prompted angry rebukes from several liberal members. He had earlier said that the motion to remove the president had no chance of success.
Some politicians hope Ilyukhin's motion may help clarify the legal basis for the succession in case of illness.
The communists have long criticised the concentration of power in the president's hands under the 1993 constitution drawn up under Yeltsin and approved in a referendum.

Yeltsin's recent incapacity has prompted some calls even among his supporters for parliament to be given greater authority. Some liberals fear Yeltsin's successor could be a hardline communist or nationalist and that it would be better to dilute the presidential mandate now.
